extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, geologists, and scientifically literate readers (19th-century/academic readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Expository guidance on observing, classifying, and explaining volcanic forms and phenomena, including morphological diagnostics, eruption indicators, product composition, and theories of origin. Aimed at informing geognostic (geological) description and interpretation of volcanoes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality of rock-nature across climates
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature of rocks, or the mixture (grouping) of simple minerals into granite, gneiss, and mica slate, or into trachyte, basalt, and dolerite, is independent of existing climates, and is the same under the most varied latitudes of the earth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing volcanic and plutonic rocks from different latitudes, expect the same mineral assemblages and structural laws; climate should not be taken as an explanatory variable for primary rock types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform laws of crustal configuration
rubrics_metrics.description: The same laws of configuration regulate the reciprocal superposition of the strata of the earth's crust, cause them to penetrate one another in the form of veins, and elevate them by the agency of elastic forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these structural laws to interpret strata relationships, vein emplacement, and uplift phenomena in volcanic districts; analogous structures are manifest across regions and even on the Moon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy of volcanic morphology across planets
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms of volcanoes (cones, craters, fissures) can be recognized even where water and air are absent (e.g., lunar craters), indicating the effects produced by the reaction of the interior on the surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative morphology (terrestrial vs lunar) can provide evidence of interior-surface interactions; absence of atmosphere does not preclude recognizing volcanic configuration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin by sudden elevation rather than gradual accumulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mountains termed volcanoes are not formed by gradual accumulation of ejected lava currents, but rather as a general consequence of the sudden elevation of soft masses of trachyte or labradoritic augite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret cone formation with consideration of uplift processes (craters of elevation) as well as eruptive deposits; not all cones imply slow surface accretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between elevation and eruption frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Eruptions are more frequent in low than in elevated volcanoes; loftier volcanoes are characterized by long intervals of quiet (whole centuries between eruptions in high Andean colossi).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use elevation as a statistical predictor of eruption frequency, but account for exceptions due to variations in subsurface channel permanence and connectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Channel connectivity affects eruption recurrence
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in eruption frequency may depend on the permanence of connections between volcanic foci and the crater; channels can be closed for a time in lower volcanoes, reducing eruption frequency without implying extinction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing activity status, consider transient blockage of conduits as an explanatory factor for quiescence rather than assuming reduced magmatic supply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eruptions commonly occur from lateral fissures
rubrics_metrics.description: Eruptions from the crater are very unusual in many mountains; eruptions generally occur from lateral fissures whenever the sides of the upheaved mountain are least able (from configuration/position) to offer resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect flanks and fissure systems for likely eruption sites; historical accounts of summit eruptions may be exceptional rather than normative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cones of eruption and hornitos alignment along fissures
rubrics_metrics.description: Cones of eruption are sometimes uplifted on fissures; larger cones (erroneously termed 'new volcanoes') line the direction of a fissure and smaller 'hornitos' are grouped together covering districts with dome-like forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map linear alignments of cones/hornitos to infer fissure directions and recent eruptive loci; distinguish large aligned cones from scattered small hornitos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence or presence of lava streams depends on local conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: In some high plateau volcanoes (e.g., Andes), eruptions of ignited scoriae with detonations may produce no lava streams; Java volcanoes show that form/position/height are not sole causes of lava-stream absence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on cone morphology to predict lava-flow generation; consider interior temperature, composition, and vent geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cone-of-cinders and crater dimensions are individual character elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The height of the cone of cinders, and the size and form of the crater yield an especial and individual character to volcanoes, although they are independent of the dimensions of the mountain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure cone and crater metrics independently from mountain height when classifying volcanoes; relative proportions (cone-to-mountain) vary widely and are diagnostic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse relation (general) between crater dimensions and mountain elevation
rubrics_metrics.description: It may be remarked in general, although liable to exceptions, that the dimensions of a crater are in an inverse ratio to the elevation of the mountain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the inverse crater-size/elevation relationship as a rule-of-thumb, not a strict law; verify with local measurements and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of imminent eruption (observable indicators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs include sudden fusion of snow at the cone, glowing heat of cone walls before smoke is visible, long narrow fissures emitting vapors, small rounding hollows of molten masses opening and closing, bottom of crater rising and sinking, and small local earthquakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple concurrent indicators (thermal, seismic, fumarolic) to assess eruption imminence; individual signs may be ephemeral or misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish openings from crater enclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Openings (cones of eruption) that rise from the bottom of the crater must not be confounded with the crater which incloses them; they are distinct features with different origins and behaviors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When documenting crater morphology, separately record interior eruptive cones and the surrounding crater rim; conflation leads to misinterpretation of eruptive style and dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crater accessibility during certain eruptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Lava sometimes streams forth from open fissures and small hollows without breaking through or escaping beyond the sides of the crater; newly-opened terrestrial streams generally flow quietly and the crater may remain accessible even during eruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess hazards locally: eruptive lava flowing within crater boundaries may allow closer observation than break-through flows; do not assume all eruptions close off crater rims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volcanic storm phenomena (atmospheric electricity & lightning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hot streams rising from the crater condense into clouds; sudden condensation and formation of large volcanic clouds increase electric tension, producing forked lightning and rolling thunder distinct from interior detonations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between atmospheric electrical storms associated with eruption plumes and subsurface/explosive sounds; recognize lightning hazards around eruptive columns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ash columns as indicators of earthquake termination
rubrics_metrics.description: Ashes, which sometimes darken the air for hours and days and adhere to vegetation, indicate by their columnar ascent, impelled by vapors, the termination of every great earthquake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ash plume dynamics can signal seismic/eruption coupling; use plume observations to infer timing of major subterranean disturbances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of observed flames and radiance
rubrics_metrics.description: Flames and radiance seen in eruptions are not due to hydrogen combustion but are reflections from molten masses projected into the air and from burning depths producing glowing vapors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining luminous phenomena in eruptions, favor optical/reflection explanations over assumptions of gas combustion unless chemical evidence indicates otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subterranean reservoirs and meltwater hazards
rubrics_metrics.description: Masses of snow by sudden fusion during eruptions cause inundations and torrents that carry scoriae and ice; infiltration converts cavities into subterranean reservoirs that may suddenly open, ejecting water, fish, and tufaceous mud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include meltwater-induced lahars and sudden ejection of reservoir contents in hazard assessments for high-elevation volcanoes; historical accounts (fish ejected, mudflows) illustrate these risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish volcanic vs indirectly connected water/mud flows
rubrics_metrics.description: Water and mud that flow from hollows in the trachytic mass, not from the crater itself, are indirectly connected with volcanic activity and should not strictly be classed among volcanic phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify secondary hydromagmatic and slope-instability flows separately from primary eruptive products when compiling volcanic inventories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mineralogical products of volcanic activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing volcanoes produce certain metals (iron, copper, lead, arsenic, selenium) and fumarolic vapors cause sublimation of chlorides and other salts which fill cavities and fissures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fumarolic sublimates and enclave mineralogy as diagnostic evidence of vent chemistry and temperature; sample crater margins and fumaroles for such phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation of volcanic glassy products with vent elevation
rubrics_metrics.description: Vitreous volcanic formations (obsidian, pearl-stone, pumice) may be entirely absent in some volcanoes, while in others they only proceed from the crater or from very considerable heights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record vertical distribution of pyroclastic glassy products; their presence/absence can indicate eruption column height and magma properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mineral composition depends on host rock, vent height, and interior temperature
rubrics_metrics.description: The mineral composition of lava differs according to the crystalline rock of which the volcano is formed, the height of the eruption point, and the temperature condition of the interior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct crystallographic and chemical analyses to explain compositional differences; field observations alone are insufficient for full mineralogical interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between Plutonic and volcanic rock formation
rubrics_metrics.description: The greater or less pressure under which softened or wholly liquid fluids are solidified appears to constitute the main difference in the formation of Plutonic and volcanic rocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying igneous rocks, consider pressure of solidification (deep-seated slow cooling vs surface/near-surface rapid solidification) as key factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lava definition and behavior in forming strata
rubrics_metrics.description: The mineral mass which flows in narrow, elongated streams from a volcanic opening is called lava; where many such currents meet and are arrested they expand in width and solidify in superimposed strata.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map lava flow networks and their coalescence to understand the formation of layered igneous sequences in volcanic fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Xenoliths and incorporated broken-through rocks
rubrics_metrics.description: Rocks merely broken through by volcanic action are often enclosed in igneous products (e.g., angular fragments of feldspathic syenite in augitic lava).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and document xenoliths to reconstruct crustal composition and the nature of rocks penetrated by magmas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification: central versus linear volcanoes
rubrics_metrics.description: Volcanoes are characteristically classified as central (a central point with many active mouths distributed in all directions) and linear (vents lying at some distance from one another forming chimneys along an extended fissure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use spatial distribution of vents and vent alignments to classify volcanic systems; further subdivide linear volcanoes into submarine cones and high-ridge summit chains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volcanic chains indicate subterranean communications and mutual dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: In volcanic chains (e.g., Andes, Mexican highlands) separate volcanoes may be mutually dependent and volcanic activity may move along them in a direction for centuries; the focus of action lies below the whole highland with only certain mountains as surface channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret aligned volcanic activity and correlated eruptions as evidence of deep-seated, extended magmatic systems; mapping alignments and rock types (dolerite, melaphyre, trachyte, andesite) helps locate seat of activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and mythic accounts as interpretive aids and cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient views (Plato, Ovid, Aristotle, Strabo) offer geognostic fantasies that sometimes align with observed phenomena (e.g., wet mud eruptions, domal uplifts) but must be weighed against empirical observation and modern theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical descriptions as hypotheses or analogies to test with observation and measurement, but avoid uncritical acceptance of mythic explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability of crater margins over decades
rubrics_metrics.description: Marginal ledges of craters vary much less than supposed; comparative measurements (e.g., Saussure vs Humboldt at Vesuvius over 49 years) can show little change in crater rim elevation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform repeated, precise topographic measurements to assess long-term morphological change rather than relying on anecdotal reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical theories of volcanic heat must be critiqued by mass/density balances
rubrics_metrics.description: Chemical hypotheses (e.g., hydrogen evolution, atmospheric inhalation) face difficulties when confronted with Earth's mean density, absence of hydrogen in gaseous emanations, and the scale of activity; modern geognosy favors increased temperature with depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate origin-of-heat theories using quantitative constraints (density, gas composition, scale of eruptions) rather than solely chemical speculations.
